pr_title: core/mount: mount command may fail after adding the corresponding proc mountinfo entry
pr_body:
Hopefully fixes #17617.

(I have not tested this yet.)
pr_comments:
> Hopefully fixes #17617.
> 
> (I have not tested this yet.)

And likely #17545.

I'm sorry, I don't quite get how this commit works.
Can you explain your thinking on the state processing here please.

There are a couple of things that confuse me.

The statement "adding the corresponding proc mountinfo" is misleading because proc mountinto is generated from the kernel mount table structures on access, there's no adding of entries as such.

Is this a little racy in that the SIGCHLD and events received when the proc mounts changes both call mount_process_proc_self_mountinfo() so how does the state end up being correctly processed, is there a possible call ordering race?

@raven-au When a .mount unit is successfully started, the state of the unit becomes `MOUNT_MOUNTING` -> `MOUNT_MOUNTING_DONE` -> `MOUNT_MOUNTED`. More specifically, `mount_start()` invokes `mount` command and sets the state to `MOUNT_MOUNTING` first. Then, before `mount` command exits, by a libmount event, `mount_process_proc_self_mountinfo()` sets the state to `MOUNT_MOUNTING_DONE`. Finally, when `mount` command finished, in `mount_sigchld()` sets the state to `MOUNT_MOUNTED`.

- `MOUNT_MOUNTING`: `mount` command is running, and the corresponding mountinfo entry has not been added yet.
- `MOUNT_MOUNTING_DONE`: `mount` command is still running, and the mountinfo entry has already added.
- `MOUNT_MOUNTED`: `mount` command successfully finished.

However, I have not checked the code of fuse or something corresponding though, if once `mount` command makes kernel to add the mountinfo entry (thus state is changed `MOUNT_MOUNTING` -> `MOUNT_MOUNTING_DONE`), and then fails with some reason, and removes the mountinfo entry, previously `mount_process_proc_self_mountinfo()` does not change the state and it is kept as `MOUNT_MOUNTING_DONE`. Thus, even if the subsequent `mount_sigchld()` detects the failure, the state is changed `MOUNT_MOUNTING_DONE` -> `MOUNT_MOUNTED`.

This patch makes `mount_process_proc_self_mountinfo()` set the state back to `MOUNT_MOUNTING_DONE` -> `MOUNT_MOUNTING` when the corresponding mountinfo entry is removed due to an error in `mount` command. Thus, the subsequent `mount_sigchld()` correctly changes the state to `MOUNT_MOUNTING` -> `MOUNT_FAILED` with `mount_enter_dead()`.

When the `mount` command is directly invoked by a user (and when it succeeds), the state of the corresponding .mount unit directly changes `MOUNT_DEAD` -> `MOUNT_MOUNTED` in `mount_process_proc_mountinfo()`.

When fuse.sshfs fails, then it should be `MOUNT_DEAD` -> `MOUNT_MOUNTED` -> `MOUNT_DEAD`. As the corresponding mountinfo is added first, and then removed. Note that even if `mount` command fails, the .mount unit does not enter failed state. But this is consistent to the case of failure in 'normal' mount, as it does not update mountinfo, so the libmount event is not triggered, thus, the state is still in `MOUNT_DEAD`.

Thanks very much for the effort describing the mount state behaviours.
That will be helpful to me going forward, ;)

> Thanks very much for the effort describing the mount state behaviours.

I could review the change if you need me too but I've really only tested this rather than looked closely at the source behaviours.
Let me know if you need me to do anything in support of this change.

> > Let me know if you need me to do anything in support of this change.
> 
> @raven-au Any kind of helps are always welcome.

I'm sorry, but after reviewing the code I find the approach used a bit counter intuitive.

The handling of the success or failure of a mount command is really the job of the SIGCHLD handler and setting the mount state in the proc mountinfo handling to influence the SIGCHLD processing seems like it's the wrong way to fix this.

I think the right place to check for and handle the exec failure is actually in the SIGCHLD handler.

This patch seems to work too.

```commit 626c81e19dd2894d945f1246178a6e24df430882
Author: Ian Kent <raven@themaw.net>
Date:   Sun Nov 22 07:42:35 2020 +0800

    mount: fix failed mount detection in sigchld processing
    
    The SIGCHLD processing of a mount failes to take account of the case
    where a mount can be set to MOUNT_MOUNTING_DONE via the proc mountinfo
    processing but the mount command ultimately fails.
    
    Fix this by checking for a mount command failure in the SIGCHLD case
    processing of MOUNT_MOUNTING_DONE.

diff --git a/src/core/mount.c b/src/core/mount.c
index faa2cb0e03..3053a75240 100644
--- a/src/core/mount.c
+++ b/src/core/mount.c
@@ -1402,7 +1402,11 @@ static void mount_sigchld_event(Unit *u, pid_t pid, int code, int status) {
                 break;
 
         case MOUNT_MOUNTING_DONE:
-                mount_enter_mounted(m, f);
+                /* The mount may have appeared in the mount table but ultimately failed. */
+                if (f == MOUNT_SUCCESS)
+                        mount_enter_mounted(m, f);
+                else
+                        mount_enter_dead(m, f);
                 break;
 
         case MOUNT_REMOUNTING:
```

> @raven-au Yes, your patch should also work. And, actually I initially thought to use your approach. However, at least in the current logic, pid1 honors the entries in /proc/self/mountinfo rather than the exit status of `mount` command. That is, even if `mount` command fails, the corresponding mount entry exists in /proc/self/mountinfo, then pid1 treats that the .mount unit should be in mounted state. Or, even if `mount` command succeeds, the corresponding mount does not exist in /proc/self/mountinfo, then the .mount unit enters failed state. See the comment in `mount_sigchld()`:

Arrrh yes.

Your saying you don't want to have to trust the execed command.
Sadly that type of problem has happened to me all too often with autofs so I agree with your reasoning.

snip ...
 
> So, in the case of the issue #17617, mount state should be correctly updated based on /proc/self/mountinfo, I think.

Yes, that does make sense even though it looks unintuitive, it caught me out, ;)

issue_context.title: Mount unit enters active (mounted) state when mount process exits with status=1/FAILURE
issue_context.body:
**systemd version the issue has been seen with**
 > Systemd 246

**Used distribution**
 > Debian Bullseye

**Linux kernel version used**
 > `5.8.0-2-amd64 #1 SMP Debian 5.8.10-1`

**CPU architecture issue was seen on**
 > amd64

**Expected behaviour you didn't see**
 > When the mount process exits with a non-zero status, I would expect the mount unit to enter failed state accordingly. Interestingly, when an unmount fails (eg `target is busy` which returns `status=32/n/a`) it does register as failed: the next line in the log reads `"<unitname>.mount: Failed with result 'exit-code'.`, and the `OnFailure` dependency is triggered. I honestly don't know whether it's intended/expected that a failed attempt to unmount a filesystem that's not mounted causes the mount unit to enter a failed state, but I would certainly expect a failed *mount* process to do so.

**Unexpected behaviour you saw**
 > When the mount process returns  `status=1/FAILURE`, the mount unit enters state `active (mounted)` and the `OnFailure` dependency is not triggered (but the filesystem is of course not mounted). I found this particularly surprising given that the log shown by journalctl indicates the mount process exit status as "FAILURE".

**Steps to reproduce the problem**
 > In my case, it's an sshfs mount triggered by an automount unit. Making the ssh key inaccessible will cause the mount process to fail (`Connection reset by peer`), triggering the bug. I have not tested with other filesystems, or with other failure modes yielding different exit codes than the ones mentioned above.
comments: Could you provide debugging logs for the issue?

Sure thing!
Attached is a recent sample from `journalctl`.

Also, in case it's relevant and helpful, a few details about my configuration:
* I have `TimeoutIdleSec=5min` set in the automount unit to automatically unmount the mount when it's not in use.
* I have a template service that executes `systemctl restart` on the *automount* unit after a 10 second delay, which is triggered by the *mount* unit's `OnFailure` directive, in order to return the automount to an idle/waiting state without manual intervention in the event of the server being temporarily unavailable.
* As you can see in the automount log, two polling processes ("pool" and "gvfs-udisks2-volume-monitor") keep triggering the automount, which is not a behaviour I intend or want. I haven't got to the bottom of this yet, but my investigation so far suggests that it may be a side-effect of the automount being located in `/media`. For now, it provides *lots* of activity for the log files!
[automount-log.txt](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/files/5549468/automount-log.txt)
[mount-log.txt](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/files/5549472/mount-log.txt)

Thanks, but unfortunately these are not debug log. Please enable debug mode by `sudo systemd-analyze log-level debug`, then start/stop the corresponding .mount or .automount unit, and provide the relevant journal log. Thank you.

Oh, I see. Sorry about that.

Let's try this again:

[automount-debuglog.txt](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/files/5550108/automount-debuglog.txt)
[mount-debuglog.txt](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/files/5550110/mount-debuglog.txt)

By the way:
* I have verified that moving the automount location out of `/media` makes the frequent polling events go away.
* Triggering the automount manually with `ls` *does* still result in the `status=1/FAILURE` → `Mounted` behaviour. (That is, with the ssh key unavailable in order to make the mount fail for testing purposes.)
* I can get you debug logs without all the noise of those polling events if you like.
@scruloose I've created #17631, though I have not tested it. If it is possible and you want, please test the PR. Thank you.

Thanks! That was quick!

In theory, I'm happy to test it. In practice, building and installing something as big and complex as systemd straight from the git repo is pushing the boundaries of my skills.

I may spin up a VM, make sure I can reproduce the bug, and take a stab at building and testing that PR at some point in the next few days. I'm not going to promise results, though.

> @scruloose I've created #17631, though I have not tested it. If it is possible and you want, please test the PR. Thank you.

Hi, I built systemd with your patch and did some testing.
I'm using a Fedora rpm based on v245.

@scruloose made the ssh key unavailable to duplicate this, the target host key not being present in the root users known hosts file has the same effect and is what I used for testing.

I didn't reproduce the problem before testing with the patch because I have seen similar sshfs mount problems before.

I see that the patch does seem ensure the mount enters the correct state on failure, the journal reports the mount failure and the mount unit status shows "Active: failed (Result: exit-code)" while the automount unit shows "Active: active (waiting)" ready to try again.

I also performed a simple test on what happens with mounts performed outside of systemd for which the proc mounts processing creates mount units.

I used a simple autofs indirect mount map and observed that an automounted mount ended up in the correct state on success:
[raven@localhost ~]$ systemctl status test-Public.mount
● test-Public.mount - /test/Public
     Loaded: loaded (/proc/self/mountinfo)
     Active: active (mounted) since Wed 2020-11-18 17:20:39 AWST; 1min 36s ago
      Where: /test/Public
       What: shadow:/Public

Attempting an automount for an autofs map key that didn't exist also worked correctly but that's because, in this case, no mount is even attempted. I also tried using an autofs map entry that would trigger an actual mount that would fail and again that worked fine with no mount unit created again because no mount actually succeeded so no mount was ever present in the proc mount table.

So the change here appears to work fine and looks to be robust.

So, did i get this right? the mount binary invocation failed, but the actual mount point is registered in the kernel (i.e. appears in /proc/self/mountinfo?)

If so, this is expected behaviour. We will track the process failing, and we'll log about it and track it. But key is: the mount is up, so we show it as active. And that's enough for us, and I think correct behaviour.

> So, did i get this right? the mount binary invocation failed, but the actual mount point is registered in the kernel (i.e. appears in /proc/self/mountinfo?)

Almost, for these sshfs mounts, one way or another, sshfs is invoked.

sshfs performs the fuse mount and then raises an ssh connection to the target host in order to use the established socket to communicate between the host and the local fuse file system.

What has happened in a couple of issues is that the socket connection fails and the fuse mount is then umounted.
It appears this appearing and shortly after disappearing mount entry confuses systemd a bit leaving the unit in an unexpected state.

> 
> If so, this is expected behaviour. We will track the process failing, and we'll log about it and track it. But key is: the mount is up, so we show it as active. And that's enough for us, and I think correct behaviour.

I think that was the complaint, the mount isn't actually up, it failed but that isn't properly reflected in the unit state.

The other complaint (in another related issue) was about the lack of logging so the user knows what's going on but it seems to me that isn't a systemd problem as I'm pretty sure that systemd will log exec'ed mount command output and sshfs must be silent about these failures (haven't actually checked).
so if sshfs failed, why did it leave the fuse mount in place? it should just have torn it down again
i don't think this deserves the 247 milestone. I am not even sure we should really do anything in systemd about this at all.

> so if sshfs failed, why did it leave the fuse mount in place? it should just have torn it down again

@poettering sshfs does so. Please read https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/17631#issuecomment-729489847.

> i don't think this deserves the 247 milestone. I am not even sure we should really do anything in systemd about this at all.

@poettering Could you reconsider this issue and review #17631?
